description:
## What happens

A heredoc interpolates, including when it is the argument to `@doc` or `@moduledoc`. That is consistent -- a heredoc is a string literal and fz string literals interpolate -- but it means documentation that *describes* interpolation executes it instead:

```
  @moduledoc """
  ... every interpolated value, since `"a#{x}b"` lexes to
  `"a" <> Kernel.to_string(x) <> "b"`.
  """
```

`x` is not bound. Nothing reports that. The module compiles, and two fixtures that had nothing to do with the edit changed behaviour:

- `protocol_without_impl` stopped emitting `artifact/incomplete-semantic-plan` on all three doors.
- `heredoc` failed on all three doors.

Both pass with the same file's documentation reverted, and pass again with the interpolation escaped as `\#{x}`. The only difference between passing and failing is the text of a `@moduledoc`.

## Why this is P1

Not the interpolation -- that is the language working as specified. The problem is that **an unbound name in an interpolation produces no diagnostic**. It does not fail to compile, it does not warn, it does not name `x`. It silently produces a different program, and the damage surfaced two fixtures away from its cause. A documentation string is the last place a reader expects to find executable code, so the silence is what makes this dangerous rather than merely surprising.

Compare `Enum.sort(1..3)`, which panics loudly with an assertion (fz-5xp.95). That is the right failure mode. This is the wrong one.

## What is correct today

Escaping works and matches Elixir: `\#{x}` in the source stores `#{x}`, and `dbg` re-escapes it for display, so the stored documentation reads correctly. So there is a right way to write this; there is just no signal when you get it wrong.

## Acceptance

- An interpolation naming an unbound variable is a diagnostic with a span, wherever it appears -- in a `@doc`, a `@moduledoc`, or ordinary code.
- A fixture pins it.

## Found how

Writing Elixir-shaped documentation for `StringChars`, whose whole subject is interpolation, so its doc naturally contained `#{x}`. The full fixture matrix caught the fallout; nothing about the edit itself suggested a behaviour change was possible.
title: [BUG] An unbound name interpolated inside a @doc heredoc silently mis-compiles the module
